name: Disakisperma
look_here_first: GREEN SPRANGLETOP: look for a usually PERENNIAL, often robust bunch with relatively broad bluish-green blades and a terminal head of about 2–15 long slender branches, frequently widely spreading or gently drooping. Branches carry spikelets mostly on ONE side. Then examine ONE mature 4–12 mm spikelet at 10–20×: commonly 4–13 florets (count inside one spikelet), with fairly blunt or NOTCHED, generally awnless or minutely pointed lemmas ~3.5–5 mm long. At the blade–sheath junction verify a SHORT MEMBRANOUS ligule with a fringed margin; in lower sheaths look for optional HIDDEN self-pollinating (cleistogamous) flowers. A flowering-head photo alone cannot prove florets, notches, ligule or hidden heads.

priority: Follow a whole rooted perennial bunch and look at flowering head with only ~2–15 relatively long branches
Note ONE-SIDED (secund) spikelets lining branches, but do not count branches as florets
Under 10–20× count 4–13 FLORETS in one 4–12 mm mature spikelet and locate broad/notched lemma tips
Check short fringed true membrane ligule; if present, hidden closed lower-sheath inflorescences support a key ID
recognition.warning: The original 2 broad arrows and the two new Commons source references do not substantiate precise florets, notched lemmas, fringed ligule, or enclosed panicles.

comparison_lesson.title: Green versus mucronate sprangletop: perennial big-floret vs annual fine-branched
comparison_lesson.memory_rule: PERENNIAL BUNCH + 2–15 OFTEN SPREADING ONE-SIDED BRANCHES + ONE 4–12 mm 4–13-FLORET SPIKELET + BLUNT/NOTCHED LEMMA points to green sprangletop. Dinebra often annual, finer-branched, with ~2–4 mm fewer-flowered spikelets.
quick_split: DINEBRA PANICEA subsp. MUCRONATA (mucronate sprangletop): generally a slender ANNUAL with MANY fine ascending branches, tiny ~2–4 mm spikelets with typically 2–4 florets and a much smaller lemma; Green sprangletop is a usually larger PERENNIAL with about 2–15 often widely spreading branches and ~4–12 mm spikelets with 4–13 florets. Both may bear four-flowered spikelets: measure the actual mature spikelet AND inspect rooted habit before deciding. DIPLACHNE FUSCA (bearded sprangletop) can also have long spreading branches; its ligule tends to be much longer and pointed (often ~2–8 mm), and lemma tip shape differs, so confirm with a microscope. Old Leptochloa dubia and Diplachne dubia refer to the same green sprangletop taxon, not new cards. Do not mistake a single branch of the panicle for a whole spikelet.
comparison_lesson.guardrail: Only D. dubium installed. Old Leptochloa dubia is a synonym, Dinebra panicea subsp. mucronata remains a SEPARATE genus/taxon; preserve botanical and nativity flags.

what_to_teach_crew: NEVER count all florets on a seedhead. Select ONE mature spikelet, identify its glumes, then count the florets within.
Panicle branch is not a spikelet: green sprangletop has a branching panicle with mostly one-sided spikelet rows.
Check a rooted perennial crown. Compare annual Dinebra as a separate actual species, not a synonym.
Inspect a 0.5–1.5 mm ciliate-fringed membranous ligule and an obtuse/notched lemma; do not point to hidden anatomy in a broad photo.
Optional lower-sheath hidden flowers are a valuable training lesson. Their non-detection in one plant proves nothing.
Original picture and two exact species Commons images teach HABIT and inflorescence; special missing photos are necessary for micro ID.
visual_needs: FULL HABIT: same individual photographed from tough perennial crown (with any basal tillers) to flowering head; add a centimeter ruler and note if stolons are present.
PANICLE: entire 2–15 branch flowering head with at least one branch showing its mostly one-sided spikelet attachment and where each branch arises along the main axis.
SPIKELET 10–20×: mm ruler beside an intact 4–12 mm spikelet, glumes and rachilla visible so 4–13 FLORETS can be individually counted.
LEMMA 20×: separate a mature 3.5–5 mm lemma and show its approximately flat/square, often shallowly two-notched tip, hair placement and any tiny mucro; do not claim a long awn.
TRUE COLLAR: unfold a blade and measure membranous ligule with finely fringed apex, showing the actual blade/sheath junction (2013 treatment 0.5–1.5 mm; some regional accounts 1–2 mm).
LOW SHEATHS: on the same plant, document an enclosed cleistogamous flowering head when present; absence in one sheath is not a negative ID.
MATCHED COMPARISON: Dinebra panicea subsp. mucronata full annual plant plus 2–4 mm 2–4-flowered mature spikelet, both shot at the same scale as Disakisperma.

items.caption: This is DINEBRA, not green sprangletop. The finer brush of branches is characteristic of the generally annual sprangletop. To make a firm ID, find its rooted annual habit and tiny ~2–4 mm spikelets with roughly 2–4 florets: those tiny structures aren't established by this overview photo.

study_only_photo_links.label: Disakisperma dubium botanical reference
study_only_photo_links.look_for: GREEN SPRANGLETOP / DISAKISPERMA DUBIUM: often a robust perennial with several nearly fingerlike one-sided racemes, spikelets carrying 4–13 florets. For best confirmation look for SPECIAL hidden cleistogamous flowerheads in lower leaf sheaths, a short ciliate membranous ligule, and a mature lemma apex often slightly notched. Older name Leptochloa dubia—same taxon.

comparison_matrix.title: Sprangletop field ID — dissect one mature spikelet
rows: Robust perennial; 2–15 relatively long often diverging/nodding branches
4–12 mm spikelets, 4–13 florets, broad/notched 3.5–5 mm lemma, short fringed ligule, sometimes enclosed secondary flowerhead
Slender annual; many thin ascending branches in narrow brush-like head
Usually ~2–4 mm spikelets and 2–4 florets; glume mucro and other tiny structures demand 20×
Spreading or ascending paniculate branches overlap; inspect collar
Typically longer, pointed ~2–8 mm ligule and different mature lemma apex; reference only, not a new canonical member
Airy branching flowerheads may look similar at a distance
Usually multiple florets inside one spikelet; glume/lemma and branching details needed
